questions.q: What is an architecture review board primarily testing, per this lesson?
options: Whether the architect can recite Salesforce governor limit numbers from memory
Whether the design uses the maximum number of Salesforce Shield features available
Whether the architect can defend specific design decisions against specific challenges, including challenges aimed at NFR trade-offs, compliance interpretations, and assumptions behind the design
Whether the presentation slides are visually polished
questions.explain: A review board tests the architect's ability to defend specific decisions under direct questioning — why this target, why this trade-off, what happens if an assumption turns out wrong — not just whether a design looks reasonable on the surface.

questions.q: What structurally distinguishes a "defensible decision" from an "opinion" in this lesson's framework?
options: A defensible decision traces back to a stated requirement, its implication, and an explicit account of what was rejected and why; an opinion is a conclusion with nothing underneath it
A defensible decision is always longer in word count than an opinion
An opinion is always wrong, while a defensible decision is always correct
Defensible decisions can only be made by certified Technical Architects
questions.explain: This lesson applies Lesson 9's trace pattern directly: a decision is defensible when the requirement, implication, and rejected alternative can all be stated; an opinion is a bare conclusion with no such structure underneath it.

questions.q: In this lesson's practice format, what is the purpose of having a practice partner ask "why" at least three times in a row?
options: To waste time and make the rehearsal longer
Because Salesforce review boards are required by policy to ask exactly three questions
To test whether the architect can type three answers in under a minute
To mimic how a real board probes for the edge of what's actually been thought through versus what's being improvised, by repeatedly pushing on the weakest-sounding part of each answer
questions.explain: Repeated 'why' questioning, each time targeting the weakest part of the prior answer, simulates how a real board finds the boundary between genuine, traceable reasoning and an answer that's being improvised on the spot.

questions.q: Why does this lesson describe the "assumption stress-test" (e.g., changing a spike from 50,000 to 200,000 cases) as testing something different from whether the original number was correct?
options: Because board members always pick an intentionally wrong number to confuse candidates
Because the test is checking whether the architect understands why the decision was made and can reason about a changed condition, rather than having simply memorized a specific figure
Because changing the assumption always invalidates the original decision entirely
Because this technique only applies to compliance NFRs, not performance NFRs
questions.explain: The point of changing the assumption isn't to catch a wrong number — it's to see whether the architect's reasoning generalizes, or whether the defense collapses because it was really just reciting a memorized figure rather than understanding the underlying trade-off.

questions.q: Which of the following is named in this lesson as a common way an NFR defense falls apart under board questioning?
options: Citing a performance number with a clearly documented source and load test
Clearly distinguishing what Salesforce the vendor guarantees from what the specific implementation delivers
Treating a genuine NFR conflict as if it had no trade-off at all, when real conflicts almost always involve some cost that a board will usually spot immediately
Having a tested, evidence-based pass on every checklist item
questions.explain: This lesson specifically calls out presenting a genuine NFR conflict (Lesson 11) as though it were cost-free as a common failure pattern — boards tend to spot this quickly, since real trade-offs almost always involve some kind of cost.
